BREKAING: China now accounts for ~28% of global manufacturing, more than any other country or economic bloc.

This percentage has more than tripled since 2004.

By comparison, US factories account for ~17% of global manufacturing value added, or 11 percentage points less than China.

In 2004, the US proportion stood at ~22%, more than double China's.

Meanwhile, the Eurozone economy represents ~15% of world manufacturing, while Japan accounts for just ~5%.

China has become a critical component of global manufacturing.

tweets.text:
There are two GTM playbooks for AI companies selling into the enterprise: the Lighthouse and the Landgrab.

Lighthouse: win a few marquee customers, build social proof, and reassure the buyer who’s afraid of making the wrong call.

Landgrab: win on math, move fast, and sign the largest number of customers possible, logo be damned.

Most assume they have to educate the market, and they default to the Lighthouse. But in markets where the buyer already knows the problem and a mistake won’t cost them their job, chasing logos is a distraction.

Full piece from a16z's Joe Schmidt and Julian Marx: https://t.co/IguoXFNZs1

tweets.text:
Global investors have never been this heavily invested in the equity market.

Equity allocations across US households, pensions, insurance firms, and investment funds are up to a record 65%.

Since the 2008 Financial Crisis, this metric has surged +31 percentage points.

As a result, it now exceeds the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble peak by 8 percentage points and the peak of the 1960s by 26 percentage points.

Furthermore, equity allocations across the same group of investors from G10 countries are up to a record 57%.

This is ~12 percentage points above the previous highs recorded before the 2008 Financial Crisis and the Dot-Com Bubble burst.

Investors are all-in on stocks.

tweets.text:
AI demand is becoming a key driver of China's economy:

China's chip exports are up to a record ~$290 billion over the last 12 months.

This figure has more than doubled over the last 3 years.

At the same time, computer and component shipments are up to ~$240 billion, the highest since 2022.

Power equipment exports are up to a record ~$190 billion, with the growth accelerating over the last 2 years.

This brings China’s total AI-related exports up to ~$720 billion over the last 12 months, an all-time high.

Western demand for China-made AI hardware is surging.

tweets.text: On this day in 1694, the Bank of England was created by royal charter, born not out of financial ambition but out of desperation: the English government, broke and losing a war against France, needed money it could not raise through taxes. A group of investors agreed to lend the crown £1.2 million at 8% interest, and in exchange they were incorporated as the Bank of England and granted the right to issue banknotes and manage the government's debt. It was a quiet revolution. For the first time a nation's debt became permanent, tradeable, and trusted, which let England borrow on a scale its rivals could not match and helped fund the empire that followed. Nearly every central bank in the world, from the Federal Reserve to the Bank of Japan, descends from that arrangement. Central banks now hold well over $30 trillion in assets and set the price of money for the entire global economy.

tweets.full_text:
This chart is making the rounds as a bear case on AI capex: "the biggest spenders are the biggest drag on the S&P."

It's misleading.

The x-axis measures each stock's share of the index move (weight × return), which mega-caps dominate on size alone, over a single window ("since June 1"). 

Here's a fair test 

🧵

Using their exact window: 2026-vs-2025 capex growth vs excess return since June 1, across all 462 S&P names with capex data.

There's a mild downward tilt: correlation −0.20, R² 0.04. High-capex names have lagged over these six weeks (WULF, HUT, CIFR are plotted but excluded from the fitted line).

Extend the window to year-to-date and the slope turns positive (+0.14).

So the since-June reading is a reversal of the relationship that held all year: high-capex names beginning to give back leadership. https://t.co/CZbQRMlj7F

Whether the reversal holds will come down to execution, earnings and cash flow. 
The clearest case: the ex-Bitcoin miners building AI/HPC: WULF, CIFR, HUT, the largest capex growers here (+321% to +750%).
This is the handoff we've flagged: miners can only re-rate on delivered AI/HPC contracts and cash flow, no longer on raw megawatts.
https://t.co/UboWLmQBPx
